newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, hurt by Mars failure, sends probe to space.
newsitem.headline: Russia, hurt by Mars failure, sends probe to space.

text.p: Russian space officials, their pride dented by the failure of a $300 million unmanned mission to Mars, sent a supply rocket to the orbiting Mir space station on Wednesday and said the launch went well.

A spokeswoman at the Russian space mission control said the supply satellite had blasted off aboard a Soyuz-U rocket from Kazakhstan's Baikonur cosmodrome. "The satellite has reached its orbit. The launch was successful," she said.

The apparent success of the mission -- the satellite is due to dock with Mir on Friday -- will be welcome news both for Russian space officials and for the three-man crew on the ageing space station, where toilet tanks are close to overflowing.

"Our priority is to provide manned space flights, and we will do this despite the difficult situation in the Russian space industry," said one official, who asked not to be identified. "Unmanned flights also are important for us."
The Mars mission played a crucial role in the unmanned space programme, but the six-tonne probe crashed into the sea just over a day after the launch after a booster rocket failed.

"We've put seven years work into this," Nikolai Ivanov, head of the main operational group controlling the mission, told a news conference after the probe failed. "I cannot begin to describe how it feels."
Space officials said a commission was examining what went wrong with the booster rocket guiding the probe, which had been due to reach Mars by September next year. But there were no conclusions yet.
"Long space missions are always risky," the first official said. "Space states are cutting money for launches."
Both Mars-96 and the latest supply rocket were launched well behind schedule due to acute cash shortages in the troubled Russian space sector.
Financial problems had postponed the production of booster rockets needed to send the supplies into orbit.
The Russians are sending equipment, fuel, oxygen, water, food and instruments for Mir's crew of two Russians and American astronaut John Blaha, who have been aboard Mir since September.
The three have already had their stay in space extended by some two months after cash problems forced the postponement of the launch of the next crew, which will include a German.
Four Mir launches have been held up this year because of a cash crunch.
The ageing Mir station, launched in 1976, is the cornerstone of Russia's space programme. Space officials plan to replace it with a new international station, to be called Alpha.
An official at the Lavochkin design bureau, which built the Mars-96 probe, said work on other projects was going on according to schedule.
"We have a technical base for missions to Mars," he said. "If the Russian space agency places orders for other, we will work on them."
